dialogs.asym_help:
Most connections are not the same in both directions. A home line downloads far faster than it uploads, and on mobile the difference can be larger still.

Leave this off and one set of numbers applies to traffic in both directions, which is what this tool has always done.

Turn it on and the fields higher up the page describe DOWNLOADS only, while the fields here describe UPLOADS. They start as copies of what you already typed, so switching it on changes nothing by itself - edit only the ones you want to differ.

This is worth reaching for when an app feels fine to browse with but struggles to send: a video call, a file upload, a game that reports your actions to a server.
dialogs.buffer_help:
The buffer only matters when you set a download/upload limit. It's a queue where packets wait when they arrive faster than the limit lets through.

Big buffer = long queue: packets wait longer (more delay), but almost nothing is lost.
Small buffer = short queue: little delay, but once it fills, packets start getting dropped.

Important: the speed you set is always delivered. The buffer only changes one thing - delay vs. loss.

What to set:
  • You just want to cap the speed, delay doesn't matter → 1000-2000 ms.
  • You want to fake a slow, laggy link → enter how many ms of lag you want (e.g. 300 = slight, 2000 = very laggy). That is the most it can add: one small download may not fill the queue, several at once will.
  • You want to see packets being dropped → 100-300 ms.

Watch the test length:
  • Short test (a few seconds): with a big buffer you may see no loss - the queue hasn't filled yet. Use a smaller buffer or test longer.
  • Longer test: loss shows up once the queue fills.

0 = endless queue: nothing is dropped, but delay can grow forever. Usually not needed.

Default: 1000 ms.

dialogs.conn_search_help:
Type any text to search the process, protocol, direction, addresses and ports of every row, exactly as before.

To search ONE column, put its name and a colon in front of the value:

    port:443            one port
    port:53,8080        either of two
    port:8000-8100      a range
    ip:10.0.0.0/8       a whole subnet
    ip:!192.168.*       everything except
    proc:chrome         a process by name, or by PID
    pid:>4000           a comparison
    scoped:yes          only the rows this session impaired
    dropped:>0          only the rows that lost something

Column names: proc, pid, proto, dir, ip, port, lport, packets, dropped, down, up, bytes, scoped.

Write several and a row has to satisfy all of them:

    proc:chrome port:443 dropped:>0

The values use the same notation as the fields on the Control page, so a comma is "either", a dash is a range and "!" means "not this".

A half-typed value simply finds nothing until it is complete. The count under the table always tells you how many rows matched.

dialogs.loss_burst_help:
Real links rarely lose packets one at a time. A microwave oven, a lift, or a switch between transmitters takes the connection away for a moment, and everything sent in that moment is gone.

This field says how many packets are lost in a row on average. The "Loss" field beside it still decides how much is lost in total, so 5 percent stays 5 percent. It simply arrives in a few clusters instead of being sprinkled evenly.

Why it matters: 5 percent spread out is something most connections absorb without a visible problem. The same 5 percent in runs of twenty stalls a transfer, breaks a live connection, and sends an application down its reconnect path, which is usually the code you wanted to test.

Set 0 to spread the loss evenly, which is how this tool behaved before this setting existed.

Two limits worth knowing. A very high loss cannot arrive in very short runs, because runs that short leave too little room between them, so the log tells you what the session will really deliver. And a long run length puts the runs far apart, so a short session may not see one at all. The log says roughly how often to expect them.

"Link outages (flapping)" further down is a different thing. It cuts the connection on a fixed cycle, on purpose. This one is random and short, in the middle of otherwise normal traffic.
dialogs.match_help:
An expression is a comma-separated list of terms. Positives are OR-ed, "!" subtracts.

  value          a single value (a bare process name matches as a substring)
  a, b, c        a list
  a-b            a range, both ends included (80-88 = 80 through 88)
  >N  <N  >=N  <=N   comparisons (numbers only)
  *  ?           wildcards (chrome*, fire?ox)
  re:PATTERN     a regular expression (case-insensitive, escape a comma as \,)
  10.0.0.0/24    CIDR (IP fields only, IPv4 and IPv6)
  !value         exclude

Examples:
  chrome.exe, !chromedriver
  80, 443, 8000-8100
  10.0.0.1-10.0.0.50, !10.0.0.7
  re:^fire

An empty field means "everything". A field with only exclusions means "everything except those". A term that cannot be evaluated for a packet (a port rule against ICMP, an IPv4 rule against an IPv6 address) simply does not match.

dialogs.profile_scope_warning:
A profile stores what the link is like: loss, corruption, duplication, latency, jitter, latency spikes, link outages, the speed limits and the buffer.

These active settings will NOT be saved in the profile: {fields}.

Use 'Save file...' to store the complete configuration.

log.driver_queue: WinDivert queue: up to {n} packets / {t} ms / {kb} KB. This is the driver's own buffer, in front of this tool's. It is a ceiling, not a fixed delay: while the tool keeps up, packets barely wait in it (on an idle machine, a fraction of a millisecond). It fills only when the tool falls behind. Then packets wait longer, and once it is full the driver drops them before this tool sees them - that loss appears in no counter here. The wait is measured, and once it reaches {warn} ms, the tool warns about it here.
log.driver_still_unloading: The WinDivert driver is still unloading after another program closed. Waiting for it...
log.driver_wait: WARNING: WinDivert held a packet for {ms} ms before this tool even saw it. The driver's queue is backing up, and that is not only added delay: once the queue is full the driver throws away whatever does not fit, before this tool can see it. That loss appears in no counter here, and it comes on top of anything you configured. Narrow the traffic filter so less goes through the tool.
log.duration_reached: Time limit reached ({v} s) - session stopped.
log.ebpf_driver_queue: eBPFDivert queue: up to {n} packets / {t} ms / {kb} KB. This is the driver's own buffer, in front of this tool's. It is a ceiling, not a fixed delay: while the tool keeps up, packets barely wait in it. It fills only when the tool falls behind. Then packets wait longer, and once it is full the driver drops them before this tool sees them. When the kernel's buffer in front of the queue fills up too, packets go around this tool without being impaired. Both are counted and reported here when they happen. The wait is measured, and once it reaches {warn} ms, the tool warns about it here.
log.ebpf_driver_wait: WARNING: the eBPFDivert driver held a packet for {ms} ms before this tool even saw it. Its queue is backing up, and that is not only added delay: once the queue is full the driver drops whatever does not fit, and once the kernel's buffer in front of it is full, packets go around this tool without being impaired. Both are counted and reported here. Narrow the traffic filter so less goes through the tool.

tips.about: Version, author, licence and the third-party components this program ships with.
tips.apply: Applies setting changes WITHOUT stopping (live). The traffic filter can only be changed by restarting.
tips.asym: Real home and mobile links are rarely the same speed and quality in both directions. Tick this to give uploads their own numbers, and the values above then apply to downloads only. The boxes below start as copies of what you already set, so nothing changes until you edit them.
tips.avg_rate: Average throughput since start = total MB / duration.
tips.block: Block (drop) all traffic to matching destinations. IP and Port each take a comma-separated list. Blocking triggers on IP OR Port (an empty field is ignored). Supports ranges, CIDR, wildcards and ! to exclude. Other traffic is unaffected.
tips.block_reject: A blocked connection is refused instead of going unanswered, so the program you are testing reports 'connection refused' in about two seconds - the same as a port that is really closed - rather than waiting out its own timeout. Only connections this computer starts, and only TCP: anything using UDP, and connections coming in from outside, are still blocked in silence.
tips.buffer: Link buffer for the speed limit, in ms: how much queueing delay a rate-limited link may build up before it starts dropping (bufferbloat). 0 = unlimited buffer. Only matters when a download/upload limit or a schedule is set.
tips.chart_seconds: How many seconds of throughput history the chart keeps. Longer shows more of the past. Shorter zooms in on the last moments.
tips.col_avg: Average packet size on this connection (total bytes / packets), in bytes.
tips.col_down: Data that actually REACHED the application on this connection - what it downloaded. The unit sits next to the number and changes with it: B, KB, MB, GB. This is the same quantity the session panel calls "Downloaded (MB)". Compare it with "down seen" next to it: the gap between the two is what the tool destroyed.
tips.col_down_seen: Data the tool CAPTURED coming in on this connection, before any impairment - what the connection offered. The unit sits next to the number and changes with it: B, KB, MB, GB. With no impairment set it equals "down". With loss or a speed limit it is higher, and the difference is what never arrived.
tips.col_dropped: Packets dropped on this connection by the active impairments (loss, link outage, LAN mode, resets, ...).
tips.col_dur: Seconds between the first and the last packet of this connection in the current session.
tips.col_event_desc: What happened: the settings that were applied, or your bug marker.
tips.col_event_type: START / STOP / CHANGE / SCENARIO / BUG / RESET.
tips.col_idle: Seconds since the last packet. It stops counting when the session stops.
tips.col_kb: Total data that actually got through on this connection (delivered download + delivered upload). The unit sits next to the number and changes with it: B, KB, MB, GB.
tips.col_local_port: Port on this machine. It is what links the connection to a process. Empty for traffic that has no ports (ping/ICMP), which is also why those rows usually have no process name.
tips.col_packets: Packets seen on this connection since it appeared.
tips.col_pid: Process id owning the local port, resolved when the packet was captured.
tips.col_process: The program that opened this connection. Read once, when the connection first appeared, so a row can still name a program that has since closed. '?' means the name could not be read - try starting as Administrator.
tips.col_proto: Transport protocol of the connection (TCP / UDP / ICMP / IP).
tips.col_remote_ip: Address this machine is talking to. Right-click a row to limit the impairments to it.
tips.col_remote_port: Port on the remote side (443 = HTTPS, 53 = DNS, 80 = HTTP). Empty for traffic that has no ports at all, such as ping (ICMP) - those rows are grouped by the address instead.
tips.col_scoped: Whether this connection was in impairment scope this session - impaired, not just watched. It stays "yes" after the connection closes, as a record. The row is highlighted only while it still matches the current target. With no targeting set, every connection is in scope.
tips.col_up: Data that actually LEFT this machine on this connection - what the application uploaded. The unit sits next to the number and changes with it: B, KB, MB, GB. Compare it with "up seen": the gap is what the tool destroyed.
tips.col_up_seen: Data the tool CAPTURED going out on this connection, before any impairment - what the application tried to send. The unit sits next to the number and changes with it: B, KB, MB, GB. The difference from "up" is what never left.
tips.confirm_close: When on, closing the window during a running capture asks for confirmation first. Turn off to close without being asked.
tips.conn_search: Narrows the table. Plain text searches every column, or write port:443 or ip:10.0.0.0/8 to search one. Click ? for the full list.
tips.conn_table: Who (process) talks to whom (IP:port). 'time[s]' is the connection duration, 'idle[s]' is seconds since the last packet. Click a header to sort. The list scrolls vertically and horizontally.
tips.control_search: Finds a field or a section by name, or by its CLI flag such as --loss. Enter goes to the next match, Escape clears the box.
tips.copy_cli: Copies to the clipboard a command that reproduces the last session: the settings START and "Apply changes" gave it, its seed and its scenario. Before the first session, it copies the settings in the form. In the .exe version, the command starts with the name of the .exe file.
tips.copy_counters: Copies every counter on this tab to the clipboard, with its caption and unit, exactly as it reads here.
tips.copy_session: Copies every line of this panel to the clipboard, exactly as it reads here - including the computer name and its addresses.
tips.corrupt: Percent of packets with one flipped data bit - tests resilience to corrupted data.
tips.corrupt_up: Percent of SENT packets that arrive with damaged contents. Only used while the box above is ticked.
tips.data_down: How much data actually passed downstream (download) since start - real usage. Packets dropped by loss or a speed limit are not counted here.
tips.data_total: Sum of downloaded and uploaded data this session.
tips.data_up: How much data actually passed upstream (upload) since start.
tips.delete_profile: Delete the selected profile. Built-in presets cannot be deleted.
tips.dest: Impair only traffic to/from chosen servers. IP and Port each take a comma-separated list. Setting both narrows to traffic matching IP AND port (an empty field = any). Prefix a term with ! to exclude it. See '?' for the full syntax. Other traffic passes unchanged.
tips.donate: Support the project (voluntary). Opens donislawdev.com/support in your browser - it funds further development.
tips.down_limit: Max throughput of INCOMING traffic (download) in KB/s. 0 = unlimited. Note: ping uses tiny packets, so a speed limit barely affects it.
tips.driver_wait: The longest a packet had ALREADY been waiting inside WinDivert when this tool received it. It is measured, not estimated - the driver stamps every packet with a capture time. On an idle machine this is a fraction of a millisecond. If it grows, the tool is adding delay that appears in no other counter, because it happens in the driver's queue before ours.
tips.dup: Percent of packets sent twice - a real symptom of a poor network.
tips.dup_up: Percent of SENT packets that arrive twice. Only used while the box above is ticked.
tips.duration: Stop the session automatically after this many seconds. 0 = run until you press STOP. Applied at START only (like the traffic filter).
tips.eff_loss: How much of the traffic you aimed at THIS TOOL broke, counting every impairment: loss, speed-limit drops, blocking, link outages, connection resets and the rest. With a target set, only the target's traffic counts, so other applications cannot dilute the number. It measures damage done here, on this machine - a packet lost somewhere out in the network never arrives here, so nothing here can count it (that is what your application's own figures, or ping's "Lost", are for). Packets the tool dropped because it was overloaded are not in here either. They have their own counters, "Buffer overflow" and "Dropped at stop".
tips.eff_seed: The exact seed used in this session. Put it in the Seed field and run again to get the same randomization - the key to reproducing a bug.
tips.event_copy: Copies the selected rows (with their headers) to the clipboard, tab-separated - paste straight into a bug report.
tips.event_search: Filter the events by direction, kind or description (e.g. 'bug', 'reset', 'out').
tips.event_sort: Click a column header to sort the log (click again to reverse order).
tips.export_conns: Save the current connection list (with your search and sort) to a CSV file (bean_network_tester_connections.csv), download/upload split into separate byte columns.
tips.export_csv: Append the current counters to a CSV file (bean_network_tester_stats.csv) - for a report or analysis.
tips.filter: Which traffic to modify. 'Both directions' covers TCP, UDP and ping (ICMP). The other options narrow it down. For a single port or address use 'Target destination' below. Locked while running (STOP to change).
tips.flap: Cyclic full outages: every 'Period' seconds the link is dead for the given percent of the time. Simulates a flapping connection (e.g. weak WiFi).
tips.freeze: Freeze the table so rows stop moving while you inspect or copy them.
tips.github: The project's page on github.com: source code, releases and bug reports. Opens in your browser.
tips.internet_only: Cuts the local network and leaves the internet up: traffic to and from local addresses (10.x, 192.168.x, 172.16-31.x, link-local, CGNAT) is dropped. Loopback (127.x) keeps working, so programs talking to themselves on this machine are left alone. Careful: if your PC asks the router for DNS, the internet stops working too, because those queries are local traffic.
tips.ipv4_only: Impairments touch IPv4 traffic only. IPv6 keeps flowing normally: it is not blocked and not slowed, just left alone. This applies with the IP field empty too, which means all addresses.
tips.ipv6_only: Impairments touch IPv6 traffic only. IPv4 keeps flowing normally: it is not blocked and not slowed, just left alone. This applies with the IP field empty too, which means all addresses.
tips.jitter: Random delay variation (+/- ms), drawn separately for every packet. Ping starts to jump instead of being steady. It also lightly reorders packets. The request and the reply each get their own draw, so the wobble on ping is wider than this number - about 1.4x usually, up to 2x at the extremes.
tips.jitter_up: How much the upload delay wanders up and down, in milliseconds. Only used while the box above is ticked.
tips.lan_mode: Simulates a network with no internet access: traffic to/from public addresses is dropped, while the local network (LAN: 10.x, 192.168.x, 172.16-31.x, loopback) works. Tests how the app behaves when the internet is down but the intranet is up.
tips.language: Interface language. Switching rebuilds the UI but keeps the current session and settings. Locked while running.
tips.latency: How many milliseconds of delay to add to every packet. With the default two-way traffic filter both the request and the reply are delayed, so ping rises by about TWICE this number: 100 ms here means roughly +200 ms of ping.
tips.latency_up: Delay added to packets your machine SENDS, in milliseconds. Only used while the box above is ticked.
tips.load_config: Load all settings from a JSON file (same format as CLI: --config).
tips.log_lines: How many log lines to keep in the strip at the bottom. Older lines are dropped once the limit is reached.
tips.loss: Percent of packets that vanish without a trace. Even 5% feels like a dropping connection.
tips.loss_burst: Makes the loss set beside it arrive in runs instead of one packet at a time, and the number is how many packets are lost in a row on average. A run of losses hurts a connection far more than the same total spread evenly, so keep it low unless you are testing how an application recovers.
tips.loss_up: Percent of SENT packets that vanish. Only used while the box above is ticked.
tips.mark_bug: Inserts a timestamped marker into the log - click exactly when you see the bug.
tips.match_syntax:
Filter syntax (the same in every field):
  80,443        a list - any of them
  1000-2000     a range, both ends included
  >1024  <=80   comparisons: > < >= <=
  !53           exclusion - everything except 53
  8*  chrome*   wildcard (* and ?)
  re:^chrome    regular expression
IP also takes CIDR (192.168.1.0/24) and IPv6.
Terms are combined: any positive term matches, every ! term excludes. A field with only exclusions means 'everything except those'. Empty = everything.
tips.mtu: Drop packets larger than the given number of bytes. Reproduces the 'MTU black hole' common in tunnels/VPN/behind NAT: small packets pass, large ones vanish. 0 = off.
tips.narrow_filter: Makes the tool look only at the addresses and ports you set under "Destination targeting" - everything else on the machine is ignored, so it runs faster and keeps up with more packets. The Statistics and Connections tabs then show only that traffic. It works with plain addresses, ports and ranges. A wildcard (*), an re: pattern, or targeting only a process leaves it with no effect.
tips.nat: NAT mapping expiry: if a connection is silent longer than the given seconds, the next inbound packet is dropped (the mapping 'disappears'). Tests keep-alive. 0 = off.
tips.peak_rate: The highest throughput reached, averaged over a 1 s window (a speed limit shapes the average rate, so a shorter window would report bursts above the limit).
tips.profiles: Ready-made settings (presets, e.g. '3G network') and your own. Selecting one fills the fields above immediately.
tips.rate_unit: Which unit the Statistics page, the chart and the readout next to the speed limits show throughput in. You still type the limits themselves in KB/s, because that is the number a saved configuration file and the command line carry.
tips.reset_layout: Forget the remembered window size and position, collapsed sections and table sorting, and recentre the window. Your settings and session are kept.
tips.reset_now: Reset all active TCP connections now (for ~3 s). UDP has no reset - use loss or a link outage for it. Works after START.
tips.restore_profile: When on, the tool reopens with the last profile you picked already filled in. It does not start a capture - you still press START.
tips.row_limit: The most rows a table will show. The tables render only what is on screen, so a large limit costs nothing to draw - it only bounds the filtering and sorting work. 0 = show everything.
tips.rst: Chance that a TCP packet resets its own connection (an injected RST). TCP only - UDP has no reset.
tips.rst_cooldown: How long a connection stays reset (blocked) after an RST, in seconds.
tips.save_config: Save all current settings to a JSON file to reproduce them or use in the CLI.
tips.save_profile: Save the current link characteristics (loss, corruption, duplication, latency, jitter, speed limits) as your own profile. The remaining settings are stored via 'Save file...'.
tips.save_repro: Saves a JSON file with everything needed to reproduce the last session: seed, the settings START and "Apply changes" gave it, counters, event log, connections and a ready CLI command.
tips.scenario: A JSON scenario file changes settings in real time (e.g. after 10 s add ping, after 20 s drop the link). 'Loop' replays it over and over.
tips.schedule: Variable throughput over time. Format: time:download:upload in KB/s, comma-separated. E.g. '2:100:0, 2:500:0' = 2 s at 100 KB/s, then 2 s at 500, looping.
tips.scope_note: The traffic filter decides what is captured. Target process / destination IP / port only decide which of those packets get impaired - everything else is passed through untouched, but still counted and listed.
tips.scope_note_capture: The driver was asked to hand over only your destination's traffic, so everything here is that traffic. Turn "Capture only the targeted traffic" off in Settings to capture and count everything again.
tips.scope_note_scoped: This view is narrowed to what your targeting selected. Turn "Show only the targeted traffic" off in Settings to see everything the tool captured. Nothing about capturing or impairing changes either way.
tips.scope_view: Off (default): every captured packet is counted and listed, and targeting only decides what gets impaired. On: Statistics, the chart, Connections and both CSV exports show the targeted traffic alone. Three counters stay on the FULL traffic either way - "Queue overflow", "Dropped at stop" and "Send failed" - because those are packets THIS TOOL lost, including traffic you never targeted, and hiding them would hide the tool's own damage. The reproduction report and the JSON output always carry both numbers.
tips.seed: Random seed. Set any number so every run randomizes identically - this makes a bug reproducible. Empty = different every time.
tips.session_capture: Which traffic the driver handed over during this session. "Narrowed to the destination" means the counters and the connection list cover that traffic only, because the rest never reached the tool.
tips.settings: App settings: interface language and how many rows the tables show.
tips.show_control_search: Shows the "Search" box at the top of the Control page. With it off the box is gone and Ctrl+F takes you to the search box in the Connections tab instead.
tips.spike: Occasional ping spikes: with the given probability (%) add extra delay (ms) to a single packet. A spiked packet arrives after ones sent later than it, so this changes packet order without making every delay wobble the way Jitter does.
tips.spike_up: An occasional much longer delay on uploads: how often it happens, and how much it adds. Only used while the box above is ticked.
tips.start: Turns traffic modification on/off. Picking a preset or changing fields does nothing on its own - only START begins impairing. Requires running as administrator.
tips.stat_block: Packets dropped by a block (firewall) rule.
tips.stat_corrupted: Packets whose payload had a data bit flipped. Packets with no payload (e.g. bare ACKs) can't be corrupted - they pass through and aren't counted here, so this can be below the set percentage.
tips.stat_flap: Packets dropped by a link outage (flapping). Counted separately from loss.
tips.stat_lan: Packets to/from the internet dropped in LAN mode.
tips.stat_local: Packets to/from the local network dropped by "Internet only".
tips.stat_loss: Packets dropped because of the configured Loss. Link outages are counted separately, under Link outage.
tips.stat_loss_runs: How many runs of lost packets this session produced. Zero with "Losses in a row" set does not mean nothing was configured: either the session was too short to see a run, or the loss is 100%, so every packet is lost and there are no separate runs to count.
tips.stat_mtu: Packets dropped as too large (MTU black hole).
tips.stat_nat: Packets dropped after the NAT mapping expired.
tips.stat_overflow: Packets dropped because the queue overflowed (heavy overload). This counter always covers ALL captured traffic, even when the view is narrowed to the target: these are packets the TOOL lost, and hiding the ones outside your target would hide its own damage.
tips.stat_queue: How many packets are waiting in the queue (grows with latency or a speed limit).
tips.stat_rate: Packets dropped because the speed-limit buffer filled up (offered traffic stayed above the limit longer than the buffer holds). Counted separately from loss and from tool overflow.
tips.stat_reordered: How many packets came out of the tool in a different order than they went in. Zero with Jitter or Spike chance set means the packets were too far apart for any of them to overtake another, not that the delay was missing.
tips.stat_rst_sent: How many RST packets were injected to reset connections.
tips.stat_seen: How many packets passed through the tool in total.
tips.stat_send_failed: Packets the tool captured but could not put back on the wire - the send itself failed, for example because the connection went down or the driver refused the packet. They never arrived, and it was the tool that lost them, not the network. This is not part of "Effective loss", which counts only the damage you asked for. This counter always covers ALL captured traffic, even when the view is narrowed to the target: these are packets the TOOL lost, and hiding the ones outside your target would hide its own damage.
tips.stat_shutdown: Packets that were still waiting in the delay queue when you pressed STOP. They were not lost in the network - the session simply ended before they were released. This counter always covers ALL captured traffic, even when the view is narrowed to the target: these are packets the TOOL lost, and hiding the ones outside your target would hide its own damage.
tips.status: Whether traffic modification is running. Green = running, red = stopped.
tips.summary: What the tool is doing with your traffic right now. 'Preview' = what START will apply. 'Active' = applied now. 'Not applied yet' = click Apply changes.
tips.syn: Percent of dropped TCP SYN packets, i.e. those starting a connection. Simulates a connection that won't establish - tests retry logic.
tips.target_process: Limit the effect to chosen apps: process names, PIDs, ranges, wildcards or re: patterns (comma-separated). Prefix ! to exclude, empty = all traffic. See '?' for the full syntax. Requires psutil.
tips.tools_adapters_col_internet: Traffic to the internet leaves through this adapter, for IPv4, IPv6 or both. Read from the routing table: nothing is sent.
tips.tools_adapters_col_ipv4: The adapter's first IPv4 address, with its prefix. The details below list all of them.
tips.tools_adapters_col_kind: What kind of adapter it is: Ethernet, Wi-Fi, a tunnel (often a VPN) or a virtual one.
tips.tools_adapters_col_name: The adapter's name, as Windows Settings shows it.
tips.tools_adapters_col_note: Where an address came from, and a warning when another device uses the same address.
tips.tools_adapters_col_status: Up means the adapter can carry traffic. Click ? for what each status means.
tips.tools_adapters_col_value: What the system says. Right-click a gateway or a DNS server to limit the impairments to it.
tips.tools_adapters_copy: Copies every adapter with its addresses, in English. The text contains this computer's addresses and MAC addresses.
tips.tools_adapters_help: What the columns and the details mean
tips.tools_adapters_refresh: Reads the adapter list again. The status line says when the rows below were read.
tips.tools_diagnostics_adapters: Adds every network adapter to the copied report: its addresses, gateway, DNS servers and MAC address. Off until you tick it - read the text before you paste it into a public bug report.
tips.tools_diagnostics_check: Runs every check again. The status line says when the rows below were taken.
tips.tools_diagnostics_clean: Unloads a WinDivert driver that was left loaded. Not available while a session is running.
tips.tools_diagnostics_copy: Copies the version and every check, in English, ready to paste into the Environment report field of a bug report.
tips.tools_diagnostics_help: What each check means, and what to do about it
tips.tools_diagnostics_proxy: Adds the proxy settings to the copied report: this account's, the services' (WinHTTP) and the proxy variables, with passwords hidden. Off until you tick it - read the text before you paste it into a public bug report.
tips.tools_exprtest_expression: The expression, written as on the Control page. A comma separates the parts, a dash makes a range and "!" excludes. Click ? for examples.
tips.tools_exprtest_field: The Control-page field whose expression you are testing. It decides what the value is: an address, a port or a process.
tips.tools_exprtest_help: How the filter tester works, with examples
tips.tools_exprtest_pid: The process ID, to test that as well. Used only for the Target process field.
tips.tools_exprtest_use: Puts this expression into the chosen field on the Control page, replacing its value. A running session picks it up after "Apply changes".
tips.tools_exprtest_value: The value to test: one IP address, one port or a process name.
tips.tools_ping_address: An IP address (IPv4 or IPv6) or a host name. A name is looked up once, at Start. Enter starts or stops.
tips.tools_ping_chart: The round trip of the last pings. A red mark is a ping with no reply, a dashed line the moment the session started, stopped or changed.
tips.tools_ping_col_result: What came back: a reply, a reply with different data, no reply in time, or what Windows or a router on the way said.
tips.tools_ping_col_rtt: How long the reply took, as Windows measures it: whole milliseconds.
tips.tools_ping_col_seq: The ping's number in this run.
tips.tools_ping_col_ttl: The TTL the reply arrived with (IPv4 only). Each router on the way lowers it by one.
tips.tools_ping_copy: Copy the rows and the totals of this run as text, in English.
tips.tools_ping_count: Stop by itself after this many pings. "until Stop" goes on until you press Stop.
tips.tools_ping_every: How often a ping goes out. The next one never goes before the last one's reply came or its wait ran out.
tips.tools_ping_help: What a session does to a ping, and what this tool sends.
tips.tools_ping_size: How many bytes of data each ping carries, from 0 to 65500 (32, like ping.exe). A bigger ping shows what a speed limit or a packet size limit does.
tips.tools_ping_start: Start pinging, or stop. The ping goes on while another tab is in front.
tips.tools_ping_wait: How long to wait for each reply. A reply after that counts as lost.
tips.tools_portcheck_check: Checks whether a program could use each port now. Nothing is sent over the network.
tips.tools_portcheck_col_holder: The program that holds the port, with its process ID.
tips.tools_portcheck_col_verdict: Whether a program could use this port. The ? button explains each result.
tips.tools_portcheck_family: Which IP versions to check. A program can hold a port on IPv6 while it is free on IPv4.
tips.tools_portcheck_ports: The ports to check, written as on the Control page: 8080, or 80, 443, or 9000-9100. Up to 1000 at a time. Enter checks them.
tips.tools_portcheck_protocol: Which protocols to check. Windows sets ports aside for TCP and UDP separately.
tips.tools_sockets_col_local_ip: The address on this computer. 0.0.0.0 or :: means every address.
tips.tools_sockets_col_pid: The id of the program that owns the socket. 0 means no program owns it any more (TIME_WAIT).
tips.tools_sockets_col_proc: The program that owns the socket. Right-click a row to target it.
tips.tools_sockets_col_remote_ip: The address at the other end. Empty for a program that is listening, and for UDP. Right-click a row to limit the impairments to it.
tips.tools_sockets_col_remote_port: The port at the other end.
tips.tools_sockets_col_state: How far a TCP connection has got. Click ? for what each state means.
tips.tools_sockets_help: What the columns and states mean, and how to search
tips.tools_sockets_refresh: Reads every socket again. The status line says when the rows below were read.
tips.tools_sockets_search: Narrows the table. Plain text searches every column, or write lport:8080 or state:listen to search one. Click ? for the full list.
tips.tools_tcphealth_background: Reads the numbers once a second also while another page or tool is open. Off: only while this tool is on screen.
tips.tools_tcphealth_col_note: How long the round trip has not been measured while data goes out.
tips.tools_tcphealth_col_process: The program that owns the connection.
tips.tools_tcphealth_col_remote: The other end's address and port.
tips.tools_tcphealth_col_resent: Bytes Windows sent again since watching began.
tips.tools_tcphealth_col_rtt: The smoothed round-trip time. < 1 ms: under a millisecond.
tips.tools_tcphealth_col_state: Open while Windows counts. Ended when the connection has closed.
tips.tools_tcphealth_col_value: The newest value. In brackets: how much a counter grew since the last read.
tips.tools_tcphealth_copy: Copies the numbers of every connection on the list, in English. The text contains this computer's addresses.
tips.tools_tcphealth_stop: Takes the chosen connection off the list. Windows keeps counting for it until it closes.
tips.up_limit: Max throughput of OUTGOING traffic (upload) in KB/s. 0 = unlimited.
tools.adapters.col.name: adapter
tools.adapters.dad.duplicate: DUPLICATE - another device uses this address
tools.adapters.dns_placeholder: Windows placeholder, not a server set for this adapter
tools.adapters.empty: The system lists no network adapters.
tools.adapters.empty_details: Choose an adapter above to see its details.
tools.adapters.empty_failed: The adapter list could not be read. The line above says why. Press Refresh to try again.
tools.adapters.error_not_ready: an adapter is still getting its address (DHCP), so the system did not list the adapters. Press Refresh in a moment.
tools.adapters.help_body:
Every network adapter on this computer, with what ipconfig /all lists for it. The adapter the internet goes through is at the top, then the ones that are up.

The list is read when you open this tab and when you press Refresh. The status line says when. Nothing is sent: the list and the route to the internet come from tables Windows keeps.

Columns:
    status - Up means the adapter can carry traffic. Down, Not present and Lower layer down mean it cannot.
    type - Ethernet, Wi-Fi, Loopback (this computer talking to itself), Tunnel (often a VPN), Virtual (Hyper-V, WSL, a VPN client).
    internet - traffic to the internet leaves through this adapter, for IPv4, IPv6 or both.

Choose an adapter to see its details below: every address with its prefix, the gateway, the DNS servers, DHCP, the MAC address, the MTU and the link speed. The note next to an address says where it came from, and warns when another device on the network uses the same address.

An adapter without DNS servers of its own lists three that start with fec0:. Windows puts them there as placeholders, and ipconfig does not show them.

Right-click a gateway or a DNS server to limit the impairments to that address. That only fills in the IP field of Destination targeting on the Control page: nothing changes until you press START or Apply changes.

The first row, Proxy, shows whether programs on this computer go through a proxy. Choose it to see this account's settings (automatic detection, a setup script, a proxy server and the names that go around it), the proxy Windows services use (WinHTTP) and the proxy variables that curl, git, Python, Node and Go read. A program that uses a proxy connects to the proxy, not to your target: to impair its traffic, right-click the proxy server and limit the impairments to its address. A server given as a name is not looked up, and the tool does not look for the script automatic detection would find - nothing is sent. Passwords in an address are hidden.

"Copy report" copies every adapter and the proxy settings, in English. The text contains this computer's addresses and MAC addresses - read it before you paste it anywhere public. Right-click an adapter in the list to copy only that one, in the same words.
tools.adapters.item.name: Name
tools.adapters.log_limited: Destination IP set from the Adapters tool
tools.adapters.note_stale: The rows below were read at {time}.
tools.adapters.proxy.note.detect: Windows looks for a script on the network
tools.adapters.proxy.note.goes_here: programs using it connect here, not to your target
tools.adapters.proxy.note.name: a name - not looked up
tools.adapters.proxy.note.readers: read by curl, git, Python, Node, Go
tools.diagnostics.clean_confirm:
This unloads the WinDivert driver from Windows. The next session loads it again, which takes about a second.

If another copy of Bean Network Tester, or another program that uses WinDivert, is running a session right now, that session is interrupted.

Clean up the driver now?
tools.diagnostics.clean_needs_admin: Cleaning up the driver needs administrator rights. Start the program as administrator to use it.
tools.diagnostics.clean_windows_only: Cleaning up the driver works on Windows only.
tools.diagnostics.help_body:
Checks what a session needs before it can start. It is the same report the --doctor command prints.

Each row is one check:
    OK - nothing to do.
    Warning - worth reading, but a session can still start.
    Problem - a session cannot start until this is fixed.

The line under each row is exactly what the program found. It stays in English, so it can go into a bug report as it is.

The rows that stop a session most often:
    Administrator rights: capturing traffic needs them. Start the program as administrator.
    WinDivert driver, "stop pending": the driver is still unloading. A session can start once the last program using it has closed.
    WinDivert driver, "running" with no session open: a driver was left loaded. "Clean up the driver" unloads it.

"Clean up the driver" needs administrator rights and is not available during a session. It also stops a session that another copy of this program, or another program that uses WinDivert, is running.

"Copy environment report" copies the version and every check, ready to paste into a bug report. The report includes folder paths, and a path can contain your Windows user name.

"Add network adapters" also puts every network adapter into the report, with its addresses - what the Adapters tool shows. It is off until you tick it, because the addresses and MAC addresses say which network this computer is on.

"Add proxy settings" puts the proxy settings into the report - what the first row of the Adapters tool shows, with passwords hidden. It is off until you tick it, because a company's proxy address says which network this computer is on.
tools.diagnostics.verdict_fail: A session cannot start until the rows marked Problem are fixed.
tools.diagnostics.verdict_ok: Nothing here stops a session from starting.
tools.exprtest.bad_ip: This is not an IP address. Type one address, for example 10.0.5.7 or 2001:db8::1.
tools.exprtest.bad_number: Type a whole number, digits only.
tools.exprtest.bad_pid: A PID is a whole number, digits only.
tools.exprtest.help_body:
Checks one value against an expression, the same way a session checks every packet.

1. Pick the field the expression is for.
2. Type the expression, exactly as you would on the Control page.
3. Type a value to test: an address, a port, or a process name and PID.

The answer appears as you type. Under it you see which part of the expression selected the value, which "!" part excluded it, and how the program reads what you wrote.

Examples:

    10.0.0.0/16, !10.0.5.0/24     with 10.0.5.7           does not match (excluded)
    443, 8000-8100                with 8080               matches
    chrome, !chromedriver         with chromedriver.exe   does not match (excluded)

"Use in the Control field" puts the expression into that field, replacing what is there. During a session it takes effect after "Apply changes".
tools.exprtest.kind_unknown: The tester cannot check this field yet. Pick another field.
tools.exprtest.no_term: No part of the expression covers this value.
tools.exprtest.no_value: Type a value to test the expression against.
tools.exprtest.not_excluded: The expression only excludes, and none of its exclusions covers this value.
tools.exprtest.note_bounds_nothing: This expression narrows nothing down: it only excludes, or it covers every value or almost every one.
tools.exprtest.note_process_tree: During a session a process is also targeted when one of its parent processes matches, unless you excluded it with "!". This tester checks the expression alone.
tools.exprtest.out_of_range: This field takes numbers from {low} to {high}.
tools.exprtest.too_long: The tester takes values of up to {limit} characters.
tools.not_here: This tool is not available on this system yet. For now it works on Windows only.
tools.ping.empty: Type an address or a name and press Start.
tools.ping.help_body:
Pings an address while a session impairs the traffic, so you can see the latency and the loss arrive. Start it, go to Control, change a setting and come back: the ping goes on while another tab is in front, until you press Stop or it has sent the number of pings you chose.

What a session does to a ping:
    Latency - with the two-way traffic filter both the request and the reply are delayed, so 100 ms of latency makes the round trip about 200 ms longer. With the outgoing-only or incoming-only filter it is about 100 ms.
    Loss - it hits the request and the reply separately, so 20% of loss loses about a third of the pings.
    Corruption - it changes the data a reply brings back, and the row says so.
    Speed limit - a bigger ping waits longer in it: 8000 bytes at 64 KB/s each way take about 250 ms there and back.
    Packet size limit - on the wire a ping is its size plus 28 bytes (48 with IPv6), so with a 1400-byte limit 1372 bytes get through and 1373 are lost.
    Duplication - it does not show: Windows hands over the first reply and drops the copies.
    A program as the target - a ping belongs to no program's connection, so a session that targets a program never impairs it.
The line above the table says what the running session does to these pings.

When the session starts, stops, gets its changes applied or moves to a scenario's next step during a run, the numbers under that line show the time since then and how it differs from the time before: the average round trip and the share lost. A ping that was out at that moment counts in neither. The chart marks the moment with a dashed line, and the copied results list every part.

The numbers: jitter is how much the round trip moves from one reply to the next, on average. "95% within" is the round trip that 95 of every 100 replies did not exceed. The longest run of losses shows whether they come in bursts.

Size is how many bytes of data each ping carries, from 0 to 65500 (32, like ping.exe). Pings is how many to send before it stops by itself.

Windows waits for a reply in steps of half a second, so the wait is offered in whole seconds. A reply that comes later counts as lost: with a long latency, choose a longer wait. A name is looked up once, at Start, the way any program does, and the address it gave is shown. Round trips are in whole milliseconds, as Windows measures them. IPv6 replies carry no TTL.

This is the one tool on this tab that sends anything: echo requests to the address you typed, from Start to Stop.

tools.portcheck.help_body:
Can your program use a port? Type one port, a list or a range, the way you type ports on the Control page: 8080, or 80, 443, or 9000-9100. Up to 1000 ports at a time. Then press Check.

Each port is checked for TCP and UDP, on IPv4 and IPv6. Untick what you do not need. Windows sets ports aside for each protocol on its own, so a port can be free for UDP and not for TCP.

Results:
    Free - a program can use the port.
    In use - a program already has it. The held by column says which. Right-click the row to target that program or to leave it alone.
    In use (owner not shown) - the port is taken, but the system does not say by whom.
    Reserved by Windows - Windows set the port aside, so no program can use it. To see these ranges, run: netsh int ipv4 show excludedportrange protocol=tcp (or protocol=udp).
    Closing - a connection that has just closed still holds the port. It frees up by itself.
    Not allowed - the system does not let this program use the port. On Linux, ports below 1024 need administrator rights.
    Not checked - the system gave an answer this tool does not know. The number in brackets is its error code.

Nothing is sent over the network. For each port, the tool asks the system for it on this computer's own loopback address and gives it back at once. Who holds a port comes from the same table as the Sockets tab.

tools.sockets.help_body:
Every TCP and UDP socket on this computer: what is listening, what is connected, and which program owns it. No session is needed, so you can check which port your application uses before you start impairing it.

The table is read when you open this tab and when you press Refresh. The status line says when.

Columns:
    local IP and l.port - the address and port on this computer. 0.0.0.0 or :: means every address.
    remote IP and r.port - the other end. Empty for a program that is listening, and for UDP.
    state - how far a TCP connection has got:
        LISTEN - waiting for connections.
        ESTABLISHED - connected.
        TIME_WAIT - closed a moment ago. No program owns it any more, so its PID is 0.
        CLOSE_WAIT - the other end has closed, but the program has not closed its side yet.
        SYN_SENT - connecting, no answer yet.
    PID and process - the program that owns the socket.

Search:
    Plain text searches every column.
    proc:chrome, pid:1234 - by program.
    lport:8080, lip:127.0.0.1 - by this computer's port or address.
    port:443, ip:10.0.0.0/8 - by the other end's port or address.
    state:listen, proto:udp - by state or protocol.
    Values are written as in the Control fields: 80,443 or 8000-8100, ! to leave something out, * for any text.

Right-click a row to target its program, leave it alone, or limit to or block its remote address. That only fills in the Control fields: nothing changes until you press START or Apply changes.

tools.tcphealth.empty: No connection is watched. Right-click a TCP connection on the Sockets tab or the Connections page and choose Show TCP health.
tools.tcphealth.help_body:
What Windows measures for one TCP connection: how long a round trip takes and how much data has to be sent again.

Windows measures a round trip only from data it sent once. When the round trip of a connection that is already open suddenly grows by about 200 ms or more - as when you start a session on it - Windows sends each piece of data again after about 200 ms, before the confirmation can arrive, and measures nothing until the delay goes down. The details then say for how long the round trip has not been measured, and the connection's row is highlighted. A connection opened while the session runs is measured exactly. So start the session first, then open the connection (reload the page, reconnect).

To watch a connection, right-click it on the Sockets tab or on the Connections page and choose Show TCP health. It stays on the list until you press Stop watching, also after it has ended, with its last numbers. Up to 20 connections.

Watching needs administrator rights: Windows counts these numbers for a connection only after a program with those rights asks it to, and then counts until the connection closes. Nothing is sent.

The numbers are read once a second while this tool is on screen. Tick Keep reading when hidden to read them while you work on another page. The counters count from the moment watching began, and a number in brackets is how much a counter grew since the last read.

Rows:
    RTT - round-trip time: how long the other end takes to confirm data. Smoothed is the average Windows keeps, last is the newest measurement. Windows measures whole milliseconds, so < 1 ms is a round trip shorter than one.
    Resend timer - how long Windows waits before it sends data again. Timeouts - how often that timer ran out.
    Resent bytes - data Windows sent again: lost, not confirmed in time, or sent again before its confirmation could arrive.
    Fast resends - data sent again at once because the other end reported a gap.
    Duplicate ACKs - confirmations the other end repeated, a sign that a packet was lost or came out of order.
    Segment size (MSS) - the largest piece of data in one packet.
    Data sent / received - every byte, data sent again included.

Windows measures a round trip when data from this computer is confirmed, so a connection that only receives has no measurements. No longer counted means the connection's port was taken by a new connection, or another program turned counting off.

Right-click the remote address in the details to limit the impairments to it. Copy report copies every watched connection, in English.
